nameStory: The spring snowflake gets its charming name from its pristine white flowers that dangle like perfect little snowdrops, appearing in early spring when winter's snow may still linger. The delicate blooms really do look like nature's own snowflakes that decided to grow on stems instead of fall from the sky. It's also called St. Agnes' flower, named after the patron saint of virgins, reflecting the flower's pure white, innocent appearance.
description: Spring snowflake is a small, bulbous perennial that produces single white flowers on slender stems in early spring. Each plant grows about 4-8 inches tall, with narrow, strap-like green leaves emerging from the base. The nodding white flowers are bell-shaped with distinctive green markings near the tips of each petal-like segment. In favorable conditions, individual plants multiply to form charming little colonies of these dainty spring beauties.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white, bell-shaped flower per stem, about 3/4 inch long, nodding downward with distinctive green spots or marks near the tip of each of the 6 white petal-like segments (tepals)

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, strap-like leaves that emerge directly from the ground in a clump, bright green and smooth to the touch, about 6-10 inches long

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing bulbous plant, typically 4-8 inches tall, often forming small colonies or clumps over time as bulbs multiply underground

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, smooth green flower stems that feel slightly fleshy and bend gracefully, each supporting just one drooping flower

habitat: In New England, spring snowflakes are primarily found in cultivated gardens, parks, and naturalized areas around old homesites where they've escaped cultivation. They prefer moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, often thriving in woodland edges or grassy areas. With only 16 recorded observations in New England, they're quite rare and mostly represent garden escapes rather than truly wild populations.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in March to April, creating the main identification opportunity with their distinctive white bells marked with green spots. Leaves emerge around the same time and remain fresh and green.
seasonality.summer: Leaves gradually yellow and die back by mid-summer as the plant enters dormancy. Above-ground parts completely disappear, with energy stored in underground bulbs.
seasonality.fall: Plant remains completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts. Bulbs rest underground, preparing for next spring's emergence.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence whatsoever. The plant exists only as dormant bulbs buried in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger new growth.

funFact: Despite being called a 'snowflake,' this plant is actually closely related to daffodils and belongs to the same family as onions and garlic - if you bruise the leaves, you might detect a faint oniony scent that reveals this surprising family connection!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with snowdrops (Galanthus), but spring snowflakes have green marks on ALL six petal segments while snowdrops have green marks on only three segments and are generally smaller. Remember: snowflakes have six sides (like real snowflakes), snowdrops have three green marks.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'snowflake' can be confusing because there's also a 'snowdrop' (different genus entirely), and both are small white spring bulbs. Additionally, don't confuse this spring snowflake with its summer-blooming cousin, the summer snowflake, which is taller and flowers later in the season.
compareHints: Spring snowflake differs from its close relative, summer snowflake (Leucojum aestivum), primarily by blooming time and size - spring snowflake blooms in early spring and stays under 8 inches tall, while summer snowflake blooms in late spring to early summer and can reach 18 inches tall. Both have the characteristic green-spotted white flowers, but summer snowflake often has multiple flowers per stem compared to spring snowflake's single flower per stem.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Summer snowflake differs from its only close relative in New England, spring snowflake, by blooming later in the season, growing taller, and producing multiple drooping flowers per stem rather than just one.
